title: The Mao Brothers and the richness of Ellington's band
summary: Green says the Mao Brothers opened as jazz tappers and claims Ellington's band had the richest sound, recalling the Cotton Club moving downtown to the Zanzibar.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So, continue about the Duke Ellington Band and the basic format of the show.
Well, he would open the show with the Mao Brothers -- they would come out.
That was the first act -- first dancing act.
Yes. They was known as the Terrific Tappers, you know, the Mao Brothers. Then, of course, there was some more of the band music, you see.
Well, what did the Mao Brothers do?
What kind of dance? Were they a class act?
Well, they was jazz -- like a jazz tap dance act. They tap danced to jazz music like --
-- "Shooting High," "Got the World on a String," like that.
Their specialty was tap dancing -- they would do a variety of tap dancing, but it was all did to one style or a certain particular style of jazz, you see. And the

Duke Ellington Band -- big band, I would way, because they played the richest music there was. I mean, you know, jazz or otherwise -- McKinney Cotton Pickers -- they were still the Cotton Pickers, but I mean, you know, he had inherited the band and it was Duke Ellington's Band at that time. And they had the richest sound, you see, in jazz or any kind of music. If you put Duke Ellington's Band in a symphony orchestra, you would hear the Duke Ellington Band. The symphony orchestra would be like, I mean, picking cotton, you know. Because it was a taste of that happen. I mean, it did come into being at that time -- that's the early '30's, you know. Yes, when the Cotton Club was moving downtown, the downtown Cotton Club, you see. It was called the Zanzibar and there was a popular building there where Jack Dempsey was. He had a restaurant, you see. And then there was the Turf Club which was another type of bar -- restaurant, you know. There was a lot of health programs going on, but they wasn't publicized, you know. Just was good living -- living was becoming -- I mean, prosperity was, you know, like I say, 'Happy Days are Here Again.' I mean -- Harry Richmond -- he featured singing that.
